title: Nick Land and Conrad Flynn in Conversation: watch-along
video_label: Nick Land and Conrad Flynn in Conversation (The Dangerous Maybe, YouTube)
summary: A guide to the 3-hour-17-minute Halloween episode of The Dangerous Maybe, where Nick Land meets Conrad Flynn, the writer who made him a Tucker Carlson topic in 2025. They cover Silicon Valley and the occult, Musk, Milton and 666, Gnosticism, Calvinism, AI and intellectual property, and the blockchain. The episode ends with news that Carlson wants to interview Land, and Land agreeing.
method: There are no YouTube captions here: YouTube blocked automatic caption downloads from this desk's server. The guide was written from a machine transcript of the audio (Whisper, base English model). That transcript has no speaker labels and garbles many names, so speakers are identified from context. Quotes are kept to short phrases; check any quote against the video before you rely on it.
Every timestamp links to that second of the video. Times are approximate, within about 30 seconds. Section titles are this desk's, not the channel's (the video has no chapters).

facts.v: "Nick Land and Conrad Flynn in Conversation," The Dangerous Maybe channel (@TheDangerousMaybe), 3 h 17 min. Posted 31 October 2026 at 19:00 Israel time (YouTube upload metadata), billed as a Halloween episode.
Mikey Downs (The Dangerous Maybe; X: @JutlandGhost) and Nance (Three Billion Nances), who co-host the interviews with Land.
Nick Land, philosopher, former Warwick lecturer and CCRU co-founder, now in Shanghai; Conrad Flynn, Los Angeles writer and producer (see the Conrad Flynn backgrounder).
Flynn's October 2025 Tucker Carlson interview presented Land as a key to the occult side of Silicon Valley's AI culture. This is the first time the two have spoken.
Flynn says Carlson's team asked to interview Land and may be in Shanghai in November; Land agrees on air (from about 3:08:00). Unconfirmed beyond this recording.

sections.title: Cold open, hosts and how the meeting came about
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: The episode opens with a teaser montage, then host Mikey Downs (The Dangerous Maybe) welcomes Nick Land and Conrad Flynn. Downs frames it as the third installment of a saga that began with Flynn's October 2025 Tucker Carlson interview about Land, followed days later by Land's own response on this channel.

Downs plugs his November course on Land's book Xenosystems at Philosophy Portal. Co-host Nance (Three Billion Nances) says he is rereading William Gibson's Neuromancer; Land says he picked it up again two days earlier, which the group treats as a fitting coincidence. Downs then formally introduces the two guests, who have never spoken before.

sections.title: Is Land really big in Silicon Valley?
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Flynn retells how he came to be on Tucker Carlson's show in 2025. Downs asks the central question from that episode: Flynn claimed Silicon Valley insiders are into the occult and draw on Land, while Land was skeptical.

Land says the question is beyond his expertise, but that on a recent trip to the San Francisco area he was surprised by how many people he already knew from online contact. He adds that most of what tech people wanted to discuss with him was "quite secular," not the occult side Flynn stressed. Flynn counters that Marc Andreessen named Land in writing and that insiders told him people were into "the whole ride" of Land's work, and he says Sam Altman has made a joke about Land. Flynn says these people are more or less guarded depending on the audience.

sections.title: The "beast pulse": 666, meter and Paradise Lost
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Land tells a story from the online gematria community, people who turn letters into numbers. Revelation 13:18 is, he says, the only number in the Bible readers are told to "count." He floated a question on X about English iambic rhythm and a cipher that produces 666, and someone replied that the first line of Milton's Paradise Lost ("Of man's first disobedience, and the fruit") sums to 666 in that cipher. He calls this the "beast pulse" and points listeners to the Cyphers website, a gematria calculator.

Flynn picks up the theme of inspiration from outside the self: Milton dictating while blind, William Blake's line that Milton was "of the Devil's party without knowing it," and Robert Graves's book The White Goddess, which Flynn says Robert Plant was reading when he wrote "Stairway to Heaven." Flynn says screenwriter Roger Avary is adapting Paradise Lost. Land says Milton's poem opens with an invocation of the Muse, so even a Puritan poet frames writing as outside inspiration.

sections.title: Musk's grandfather, Technocracy, and drinking the sun
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Flynn shows a 1930s Technocracy birthday card with a giant robot whose sound is "tweet," and links it to Elon Musk's grandfather, who belonged to the Technocracy movement. He treats it as a possible case of the future leaking into the past, or just a coincidence.

Asked about Musk, Land says he has no special insight, but calls Musk a guy who "breaks the matrix" of modern capitalism, "the Henry Ford of the 21st century." He says Musk's religion is not gothic occultism but something like sun worship: climbing the Kardashev scale (a ranking of civilizations by how much energy they use) and turning solar energy into intelligence. The deeper question, Land says, is "what can the sun think?"

sections.title: How Land came to Crowley, and the Gnostic tradition
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Flynn asks how Land found Blavatsky, Crowley and Kenneth Grant. Land says he resisted at first. The turning point was that CCRU members were living in, and meeting at, a house that turned out to have been Aleister Crowley's. He says they did nothing exotic there beyond a Tree of Life on the wall, and stresses that they were "brought into" Crowley's house rather than seeking it out. He dates it to the early 1990s but can't be exact.

On Gnosticism, Land argues we are all more inside the Gnostic tradition than we realize. Gnosticism here means the ancient Christian-era belief that we are trapped in a false world and saving knowledge comes from outside it. He points to TV: Severance and Silo, both about people sealed inside a space with no access to the truth outside. He says the supposed break between traditional religion and modern culture is "fake".

timeline.text: Flynn asks about Land's path into esoteric reading.
Land: CCRU met in what turned out to be Crowley's house.

sections.title: Gnostic cinema, the tesseract and Solomon
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Flynn cites Harold Bloom's view that Gnosticism is the real American religion, then lists 1990s films on the theme (The Matrix, The Truman Show, Dark City, Pleasantville). He builds a chain: Jonathan Nolan made HBO's Westworld and co-wrote Interstellar, whose climax uses a tesseract (a four-dimensional cube). The tesseract idea was popularized by Charles Howard Hinton, whom Crowley and Theosophists admired, and Geoffrey Hinton, the "godfather of AI," is his great-grandson. Land says he has nothing to add and will have to rewatch Hellraiser.

Flynn turns to 666 in the Book of Kings, the talents of gold Solomon received each year, and the biblical idea of answering "dark sentences" (riddles), which he links to the Antichrist and to chatbots that answer any question.

sections.title: No innocent literal Bible, and the problem of unity
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Land notes the 666 references in Kings, Chronicles and Revelation and calls the gold link an "occult political economy." He then makes one of his main points: there is no innocent, purely literal reading of the Bible. Augustine gave up on a literal commentary on Genesis, Land says, partly because Adam and Eve's eyes are "opened" after Eve has already seen the fruit. Land calls himself a biblical fundamentalist but a non-literalist.

Flynn raises John C. Lilly, the dolphin and ketamine researcher who described visions of hostile "solid state entities." Land shifts to the question of unity. AI-safety thinkers fear a "singleton," one AI that takes over, and theology faces the same question, because the Hebrew word Elohim, translated "God," is plural. He criticizes Tucker Carlson's refrain that "it never ends well" as unbiblical, because the Christian story is a comedy, not a tragedy.

sections.title: The sovereignty of God, Satan and the video game
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Land says it is incoherent for a Christian to fear that Satan might win; Calvinism, which insists most strongly on God's total control, is the best guide. Flynn connects this to Norbert Wiener's 1964 book God and Golem, Inc. and the problem of evil. God can create evil and stay in control, but humans who make a golem or AI may not be able to. He uses a video-game metaphor: the designer puts the enemies in the game and is never at risk.

Land explains two Calvinist positions. Infralapsarianism holds that God's decrees of who is saved come after the Fall. Supralapsarianism holds that they were set before it, so the serpent and the Fall are part of the script. He says the tradition holds both total sovereignty and real freedom without resolving the paradox.

sections.title: Burroughs, parallel currents, Bataille and the headless god
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Flynn quotes William Burroughs's advice that any good magician uses the latest technology. Land says overlaps between CCRU and similar artists were mostly "correlation and not causation," people tapping the same current.

Nance raises Georges Bataille's "headless god" (Acéphale) and suggests AI is a headless collective will. Flynn adds Maya Deren's study of Haitian Vodou possession and the biblical "Legion" of demons: who is in charge when many forces run through one body? Land ties this to his numerology. He contrasts a system topped by a unity with one whose summit is zero, the "empty summit," and says this is the liberal tradition: Adam Smith's invisible hand, where no command center exists and that is why it works.

sections.title: Gnostic Calvinism vs Neolemurianism
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Downs asks whether Land's current "Gnostic Calvinism" is just his old CCRU "Neolemurianism" in Christian dress, since both rely on time loops (the future shaping the past). Land says he is not inventing Gnostic Calvinism any more than CCRU invented Neolemurianism; things are "coming back." He argues that apophatic (negative) theology, which says only what God is not, is the serious tradition. Downs and Flynn recommend Arthur Pink's books The Sovereignty of God and The Antichrist.

sections.title: Theosophy, Marx, and the left accelerationist view
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Flynn tells stories linking Theosophy to politics: Annie Besant, Nehru and the Indian National Congress; Truman Capote blaming Theosophy for Sirhan Sirhan. He asks about Marx's cousin and the Philips electronics company, whose subsidiary released Black Sabbath's first album, and about Land's idea that capitalism culminates in AI.

Land hands the question to the hosts. Downs and Nance describe themselves as "left accelerationists": they read Land as a "dark Marxist" whose core idea is that capitalism is artificial intelligence, the long replacement of human labor with machines. They want to defend human subjectivity without being anti-technology. Nance compares AI agents to video-game speedrunners who ignore the story and only exploit the code.

sections.title: AI and the end of intellectual property
sections.basis: Summary written by this desk from a machine transcript of the audio; speakers identified from context.
paras: Flynn says AI will "single-handedly destroy intellectual property." Land agrees that this is not a simple left-right issue, since some libertarians also oppose IP. He says nobody has a model for an economy without IP, and that answers will come "from the outside" rather than from human coordination. On the end of work, he calls both utopian and doomer talk an "antinomy," two opposite claims that both seem right, which is what you get when "crashing into singularity." Flynn compares AI remixing to 1980s sampling in music.

Flynn credits Constance Cumbey with the blockchain-Antichrist idea and brings up Jeffrey Epstein's AI interests. glossary.v: The idea that the way through capitalism and technology is to speed them up rather than resist them. "Left" accelerationists, like the hosts, want the speed-up to serve people; Land's version treats capital and AI as forces that will outgrow humans.
CCRU's word for fictions that make themselves real: an idea or story that spreads and, by spreading, helps bring about what it describes.
Land's term for whatever lies beyond human experience and control: the future, the alien, the inhuman. In this episode it shows up as answers coming "from the outside."

A term Land took from the blogger Curtis Yarvin (Mencius Moldbug) for the network of universities, media and civil service that he says sets acceptable opinion. Not used in this episode, but it is central to his politics.
The Cybernetic Culture Research Unit, an informal group around Land and Sadie Plant at the University of Warwick in the mid to late 1990s.
CCRU's number diagram linking the digits 0 to 9, used as a system of divination. Carlson held one up on air in 2025.

CCRU's name for the entities linked to the Numogram, borrowed from William Burroughs's story "The Ghost Lemurs of Madagascar." Neolemurianism was CCRU's mock-religion around them. Lemures were Roman spirits of the dead.
Land's recent label for his theology: the Calvinist belief in God's total control over history, read together with the Gnostic belief that this world is a kind of prison or simulation.
Land's image for a system with no one at the top, like markets (the invisible hand) or neural networks, that he says can direct things more powerfully than a single ruler.
Turning letters into numbers and looking for meaning in the totals. "AQ" (Alphanumeric Qabbala) is a cipher associated with CCRU.
An AI-safety term for one AI or authority that ends up controlling everything.
Two Calvinist views on whether God decided who is saved before or after deciding to allow the Fall.

checks: Flynn says Geoffrey Hinton is Charles Howard Hinton's great-grandson. That matches published family histories, but Flynn also called Hinton Ilya Sutskever's mentor "at OpenAI"; Hinton supervised Sutskever at the University of Toronto and did not work at OpenAI.

Flynn says Marc Andreessen's "book" names Land. The best-known mention is Andreessen's 2023 essay "The Techno-Optimist Manifesto," which lists Land among its "patron saints." It is an essay, not a book.

The claim that Musk's grandfather Joshua Haldeman was in the Technocracy movement and was arrested in Canada is widely reported; the 1930s "tweet" robot card was shown on screen but not independently checked here.
Flynn's claim that Robert Graves wrote a chapter of William Sargant's Battle for the Mind (1957) is unconfirmed.
Flynn's claim that Robert Plant was reading The White Goddess when he wrote "Stairway to Heaven" is unconfirmed.
The claim that a Wild Wild West episode inspired Anton LaVey's look is Flynn's and is described by him as alleged. Unconfirmed.
Flynn says Constance Cumbey died the summer before his Tucker interview. Unconfirmed.
Flynn's account of a Tucker Carlson producer asking for a Land interview, and a planned Shanghai trip in November, comes only from Flynn on this recording. Unconfirmed.

Black Sabbath's first album came out on Vertigo, a Philips label, and the Philips founders were related to Karl Marx through his mother's family. Flynn calls the founder Marx's "first cousin"; the exact relationship should be checked.
Land's account of CCRU meeting in a house that had been Crowley's is his own memory. He gives no address or date beyond "early-ish 1990s."
